_readme: Cache-first lookup content for the 15 suggested chip questions defined in frontend/app.html's DOMAINS array.

WIRED (demo cache-first path, both personas): app.services.chortlechat loads this file into _PRESET_CACHE (keyed by exact question text) and, on a cache hit, answers straight from baseline_answer or banter_answer below, whichever the request's persona asked for — no retrieval call, no confidence-threshold gate, no generation call for either persona. All 15 questions are covered, so a demo run never depends on a live vector store or instruct model for any of the suggested chips. See app.services.chortlechat's module docstring, _PRESET_CACHE, and _preset_response.

Every baseline_answer is drafted strictly from the cited passage(s) in backend/data/chortlechat_corpus.json, in Baseline's voice, using the same 'say only what the source supports' rule app.services.chortlechat._BASELINE_PROMPT already enforces. All doc_id/domain citations below were re-verified directly against chortlechat_corpus.json.

Every banter_answer is a hand-drafted restyle of that same entry's baseline_answer, written under the exact same rule app.services.chortlechat._BANTER_PROMPT enforces at generation time: personality and phrasing may differ, but every fact, number, and claim must already be present in baseline_answer. Nothing in banter_answer should ever say more, or something different, than baseline_answer already says — treat any drift caught in review as a bug in the draft, not an acceptable embellishment.

confidence is deliberately null on every entry, not a filled-in number, and stays null in the AskResponse for a cache hit too — the same meaning it already carries for 'nothing was retrieved,' which is literally true here since retrieval never runs for a cache hit.

entry 'tc-formation-conditions' (#3) has grounded: false and baseline_answer/banter_answer both null — no passage in the corpus actually answers it (see match_quality/caveat). It is still cached (use_cache: true): a hit routes straight to app.services.chortlechat._fallback_response, the same honest 'no grounded answer' text every other unanswerable question gets, without touching retrieval either. This is the one entry where 'preset' means 'preset to say I don't know,' not 'preset to a fabricated answer.'

summary.note_on_count: frontend's DOMAINS array lists 18 chip slots across 6 tabs, but 'All' repeats 5 questions that also appear under their own domain tab, so there are only 15 distinct question strings. All 15 are covered here.

entries.question: What ocean heat conditions favor tropical cyclone intensification?
entries.baseline_answer: A barrier layer thickness of 10-30 meters combined with a tropical cyclone heat potential of 40-80 kJ/cm² favors intensification in the central Bay of Bengal. As storm intensity increases, the right-rear sector of the cyclone shows the largest heat-potential anomalies, and sea-surface cooling beneath the strongest, slowest-moving storms reaches 0.5-1.2°C in the inner core.
entries.banter_answer: Picture the ocean as a fuel tank: a 10-30 meter buffer layer sitting on top of 40-80 kJ/cm² of stored heat is basically premium unleaded for a storm over the central Bay of Bengal. And as the cyclone spins up, it doesn't sip evenly — the right-rear side drains the tank hardest, cooling the sea surface there by 0.5-1.2°C right under the strongest, slowest-crawling storms.

entries.question: How does eyewall mesovortex dynamics affect a hurricane's intensity?
entries.baseline_answer: In Hurricane Ike, mesovortices within the eyewall showed a consistent arrangement of vorticity and vertical-velocity maxima wherever they formed in the eyewall. Mesovortices kept forming even after the storm's center moved onto land, though their structure diverged from pre-landfall mesovortices as the storm interacted with the coastline and weakened. The source describes this structural behavior; it does not quantify how much eyewall mesovortices change peak intensity.
entries.banter_answer: Hurricane Ike's eyewall was basically running the same choreography over and over — wherever a mesovortex popped up, the same vorticity-and-updraft pattern showed up right behind it. The show didn't even stop at landfall; mesovortices kept forming, just with a slightly different routine once the coastline started interfering. What I can't tell you is how many points that performance added to Ike's peak intensity — the source never keeps that scoreboard.
entries.caveat: Source documents mesovortex structure and behavior, not a quantified link to intensity. Answer is scoped to say only that.

entries.question: What atmospheric conditions influence tropical cyclone formation?
entries.caveat: Nothing in the corpus addresses genesis-favorable atmospheric conditions (wind shear, moisture, instability) directly. Closest passages cover ocean heat content's effect on intensification (already used for tc-ocean-heat-intensification) or the Saharan Air Layer's suppression of activity (used for saharan-dust-tc-development) — neither answers this question as asked. Cached to the honest fallback, not to a fabricated answer — see _readme.

entries.question: How does airborne Saharan dust affect tropical cyclone development?
entries.baseline_answer: The Saharan Air Layer tends to suppress Atlantic tropical cyclone activity by introducing dry, stable air into the storm, which increases vertical wind shear and the temperature inversion at lower levels. Separately, dust within the layer can act as cloud condensation and ice nuclei, influencing storm development by altering hydrometeor properties, diabatic heating distribution, and thermodynamic structure — as seen with Hurricane Erin in 2001. The relative size of these two effects, suppression versus microphysical influence, is still not fully resolved.
entries.banter_answer: The Saharan Air Layer plays bad cop to Atlantic hurricanes: it dumps in dry, stable air that cranks up wind shear and slaps a temperature inversion on the storm, mostly telling it to calm down. But that same layer carries dust that can act as cloud condensation and ice nuclei — tinkering with cloud particles, heating patterns, and the storm's structure, the way it did with Hurricane Erin back in 2001. Scientists still argue over which effect wins, the suppression or the dust tinkering — no verdict yet.

entries.question: What is the impact of Saharan dust on the atmosphere?
entries.baseline_answer: An estimated 240 ± 80 million tons of Saharan dust cross the Atlantic from Africa every year. Dust directly affects Earth's radiative balance by absorbing and scattering sunlight, and dust coated with sulfur or other soluble material can also act as cloud condensation and ice nuclei, altering cloud development.
entries.banter_answer: Every year, roughly 240 million tons (give or take 80 million) of Saharan dust packs its bags and crosses the entire Atlantic. Once it's airborne, it messes with Earth's light budget by absorbing and scattering sunlight, and if it's picked up a sulfur coating along the way, it can even moonlight as a cloud condensation or ice nucleus, nudging how clouds form.

entries.question: How are dust storms characterized by particle size?
entries.baseline_answer: Dust storms are characterized using MODIS spectral reflectance rather than direct particle sizing: the reflectance of dust (sand and soil) increases with wavelength between 0.4 and 2.5 μm, reaching a minimum in MODIS band 3 and a maximum in band 7. This spectral signature is distinct enough from cloud reflectance to distinguish dust storms from clouds in satellite imagery.
entries.banter_answer: Nobody's out there measuring individual grains of sand mid-storm — instead, MODIS reads dust by its light signature: reflectance climbs as wavelength increases from 0.4 to 2.5 μm, bottoming out at band 3 and peaking at band 7. That fingerprint looks different enough from clouds that satellites can tell 'dust storm' from 'just a cloud' without anyone measuring particle sizes at all.
entries.caveat: Source characterizes dust by spectral reflectance signature (via MODIS bands), not by a particle-size distribution as literally asked.

entries.question: How are historical droughts reconstructed from climate data?
entries.baseline_answer: Historical drought reconstruction relies on precipitation records that must first be corrected for non-climatic biases — issues like snowfall-to-liquid conversion, rain gauge placement affecting collection in wind, evaporation loss between infrequent readings, and changes in instrumentation or the physical environment around a gauge. Because undercounting is worst in the cold season, this kind of reconstruction is often restricted to the warm season (April-August) and relies on careful screening of the best available records.
entries.banter_answer: Turns out old rain gauges have baggage: snow that doesn't melt cleanly, wind blowing rain past the collector, evaporation eating readings between visits, plus decades of swapped-out instruments — all of it has to be scrubbed out before a drought record means anything. And because winter is where gauges lie the most, reconstructions usually stick to the April-through-August stretch and cherry-pick only the most trustworthy records.

entries.question: How is satellite-based precipitation data validated on the ground?
entries.baseline_answer: Satellite precipitation estimates from GPM's radar and imager instruments are compared against quality-controlled ground observations — NPOL radar, high-resolution rain-rate radar, disdrometers, and rain gauges — accounting for a fall-delay time lag between the satellite overpass and when rain reaches the surface. That lag isn't constant; it varies between 0 and 30 minutes after overpass, so this study compared satellite retrievals against the ground-based mean measured 2-8 minutes after overpass time.
entries.banter_answer: Satellites don't just get to call their own shots on rainfall — GPM's radar and imager readings get checked against ground truth: NPOL radar, high-res rain radar, disdrometers, and plain old rain gauges. There's a catch though: rain takes its time falling, anywhere from 0 to 30 minutes after the satellite flies over, so this study graded the satellite against the ground average measured 2-8 minutes post-overpass, not an instant snapshot.

entries.question: What evidence do scientists use to study climate change over time?
entries.baseline_answer: One example: researchers analyzed decades of time-series data on spring water quality and quantity using the Mann-Kendall trend test, a statistical method for detecting gradual trends in a long record. That analysis attributed decreasing spring discharge to declining precipitation (a climate-linked driver) and separately attributed water-quality deterioration to human activity such as mining, agriculture, and urbanization — illustrating how long-term monitoring records and trend tests are used together to separate a climate signal from other causes.
entries.banter_answer: Here's one way scientists play detective with climate change: take decades of spring-water records and run them through the Mann-Kendall trend test, a tool built for spotting slow-motion trends. In one case, that method pinned shrinking spring flow on falling precipitation — a climate fingerprint — while pinning the water getting dirtier on human activity like mining, farming, and urbanization. Long records plus the right statistical test, and you can tell the climate's handwriting apart from everyone else's.
entries.caveat: Reused from a water-quality case study rather than a general treatment of climate-change evidence, since the corpus has no passage framed at that general level.

entries.question: What environmental factors drive wildland fire risk?
entries.baseline_answer: Wildland fires are a major source of fine particulate pollution in the US, accounting for roughly 25% of primary PM2.5 emissions. Ignition sources differ by region — human-ignited prescribed and agricultural burns dominate in the southeastern US, while about 70% of burned area in the western US comes from lightning-ignited fires — and in both regions, burned area is closely tied to environmental conditions and can be affected by a changing climate.
entries.banter_answer: Wildfires aren't just dramatic — they're also a heavyweight polluter, responsible for about a quarter of the US's fine particulate (PM2.5) emissions. Who lights the match depends on where you are: the Southeast mostly blames people (prescribed and agricultural burns), while the West mostly blames the sky — about 70% of its burned area starts with lightning. Either way, how much actually burns tracks environmental conditions, and a changing climate can shift that.

entries.question: What causes environmental degradation?
entries.baseline_answer: Pollution is the main driver of environmental degradation. It comes from a variety of sources, including vehicle emissions, agricultural runoff, accidental chemical release from factories, and poorly managed harvesting of natural resources — and its effects include depleting resources, disturbing ecosystems, and contributing to the loss of animal populations.
entries.banter_answer: If environmental degradation had a most-wanted poster, pollution would be on it — showing up as tailpipe exhaust, agricultural runoff, the occasional factory chemical release, and resources harvested with more enthusiasm than planning. The damage isn't subtle either: depleted resources, disturbed ecosystems, and animal populations paying the price.

entries.question: How does pollution affect water quality?
entries.baseline_answer: In a study of karst spring water in China, anthropogenic activity — coal mining and quarrying, agriculture, and urbanization — was found responsible for measurable water-quality deterioration over time, tracked using the Mann-Kendall trend test on decades of monitoring data. Separately, declining precipitation linked to climate change reduced spring discharge itself, showing that water quantity and quality respond to different but overlapping pressures.
entries.banter_answer: A karst spring in China got the full human treatment — coal mining, quarrying, farming, and sprawling cities — and decades of monitoring data, run through the Mann-Kendall trend test, caught the water quality getting measurably worse because of it. Meanwhile, a separate culprit, climate-linked drops in rainfall, was quietly shrinking how much water came out of the spring at all — proof that water's quantity and its quality don't always answer to the same cause.

entries.question: What causes severe mesoscale thunderstorm systems?
entries.baseline_answer: One recognized category, high-shear, low-CAPE (HSLC) severe convection, remains hard to forecast and is responsible for most significant tornado and wind reports during the cool season, especially overnight — a period when typical severe-weather indicators are otherwise unfavorable. Its regional character differs: western US HSLC events tend to involve a drier lower troposphere and a surface triple point or upslope setup, while eastern events are more associated with low cloud bases along a warm sector or cold front, even though the broader upper-atmosphere forcing looks similar across regions.
entries.banter_answer: There's a particularly stubborn troublemaker in severe weather forecasting called high-shear, low-CAPE (HSLC) convection — it's behind most of the significant cool-season tornado and wind reports, often overnight, exactly when the usual warning signs go quiet. And it doesn't even show up the same way twice: out West it favors a drier lower atmosphere with a surface triple point or upslope setup, while back East it prefers low clouds riding along a warm front or cold front — even though the atmosphere upstairs looks about the same either way.
entries.caveat: Source characterizes high-shear, low-CAPE (HSLC) severe convection regionally rather than stating a general causal mechanism for severe mesoscale thunderstorms.

entries.question: What is a dryline and how does it trigger severe weather?
entries.baseline_answer: A dryline is a boundary separating a region of very dry air from one with much higher moisture content. Drylines matter because they act as a trigger for thunderstorms, which can produce severe weather — in subtropical southern Africa, they're most frequent over eastern South Africa in early summer, exactly when large-hail and damaging-wind storms are most likely.
entries.banter_answer: Think of a dryline as the line in the sand — literally — between bone-dry air and a much muggier neighbor. That boundary is a thunderstorm's favorite trigger, and in subtropical southern Africa it shows up most over eastern South Africa in early summer, which just happens to be prime time for large hail and damaging winds.

entries.question: What is cold-air damming?
entries.baseline_answer: The source documents a cold-air damming case where a surface anticyclone stayed nearly stationary while a low-pressure system tracked east of Jackson, Mississippi, strengthening the pressure gradient in the mountain-parallel direction along the Appalachians. That setup showed increased ridging east of the mountain crests (Virginia to Georgia) and increased troughing over and west of the Appalachians (New York to Tennessee) — the characteristic pattern of cold, dense air banking up against the eastern slopes.
entries.banter_answer: Cold-air damming, case study edition: a surface high pressure system parked itself and stayed put while a low pressure system slid east of Jackson, Mississippi, cranking up the pressure gradient running alongside the Appalachians. The result looked exactly like the textbook picture — more ridging east of the mountains from Virginia to Georgia, more troughing on and west of them from New York to Tennessee — basically cold, heavy air piling up against the eastern slopes.
entries.caveat: Source is a specific case study (a March 22 synoptic event) rather than a textbook definition; the answer describes the phenomenon through that case.
